newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 23.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- SAINTS SHARES SOLD TO CHIEFS AHEAD OF BID

Shares in Southampton Football Club, sold to directors, have soared in value from 150 to 68,880 sterling at its recent takeover. The shares were sold by an investment company, Westwood Secretaries, which was run until recently by Southampton chairman Guy Askham. He refused to reveal the identity of the beneficial vendor, or why he sold the stake when he knew a bid was in the offing.
-- SHORTS LEADS NATIONWIDE JOBS BOOST

The creation of almost 2,000 new jobs in the aerospace, postal and meat processing industries was announced yesterday. Belfast aerospace group Shorts said 600 jobs would result from a contract from its Canadian parent Bombardier for work on a 70-seater regional jet. 700 jobs will be created at a Parcelforce distribution centre in Coventry. St Merryn Meat will employ 663 at a new factory in Merthyr Tydfil, South Wales, as well as creating 70 supply roles.
-- EMU COULD HIT INSURANCE INDUSTRY FOR UP TO ONE BILLION STERLING

A report published yesterday by the Association of British Insurers warned that economic and monetary union could cost the insurance industry one billion sterling over the three-year transition period, and up to 200 million sterling even if Britain does not join. The costs would mainly come from converting computer systems and training staff. The report stressed the industry should start planning soon.
THE TIMES
-- FEARS OF RATE RISE RECEDE AS HIGH STREET SALES FALL

A fall in high street sales over the Christmas shopping period, disappointing modest expectations in the City, has given the Chancellor more ammunition to avoid a damaging interest rate rise before the general election. Retail sales fell 0.8 per cent in December. Against a year ago, sales were up only 2.9 per cent compared with year-on-year growth of 3.9 per cent in November.
-- ROYAL YACHT BRINGS HOPE OF JOBS TO SHIPYARDS

Government plans to build a new royal yacht in Britain announced yesterday topped a good day for employment, with a total of 2,500 new jobs in the pipeline. Taxpayers money will fund the new royal yacht which will be built at one of the few remaining UK shipyards.
-- TOYOTA JOBS DEPEND ON EURO-SCEPTICS STANCE

Toyota has given a warning that friction in the Government about the future of Britain's role in Europe could threaten the group's plans to invest in Britain. The company wants to make more cars in Europe with the plant at Burnaston, Derbyshire being a favorite to win new investment, creating hundreds of jobs. But Toyota states that a move to leave the European Union could have serious consequences for future investment.
THE GUARDIAN
-- SECRET MEETING TO BREAK RIGHTS ISSUE IMPASSE

At a secret meeting this week, Britain's biggest shareholders and corporations tried to overcome the logjam over new ways for companies to raise capital. Finance directors are trying to convince pension and insurance fund managers that providing a cheaper alternative to the present system of underwriting rights issues could save British industry 50 million sterling in fees each year.
-- HALIFAX TRIMS COST OF FIXING

The Halifax Building Society has cut the cost of one of the most popular fixed-rate mortgages. The Halifax, which is Britain's largest mortgage lender, says that borrowers fear interest rate rises. The cost of the five-year fixed-rate is to drop from 8.55 per cent to 7.75 per cent, making the Halifax one of the cheapest lenders.
-- BRITAIN HAS EU'S MOST MISERLY SUBSIDIES

European Union competition commissioner Karel Van Miert revealed yesterday that British manufacturers received fewer state subsidies per worker than any of their counterparts in other European Union countries. Mr Van Miert said that he would take a tougher stance on state aid cases, in a bid to reduce state aid, after provisional data showed a rise in state subsidies during 1993-94, which is the latest data available.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- HANDICAPPEDS' FIRST STEP TO SOCIETY SHARE BONANZA

A private members' bill from Conservative MP Douglas French received an unopposed first reading yesterday. The bill aims to force demutualising societies to set aside funds for handicapped members, who would otherwise be denied a share of flotation bonanzas, as they are the second-named signatories on society accounts. The second reading will be on 14 February.
-- CLYDE NOT FOR SALE UNDER 135p, SAY KEY SHAREHOLDERS

Gulf Canada's 432 million sterling bid for Clyde Petroleum is likely to fail unless it increases its bid by almost one-third, it emerged yesterday. Key shareholders are unwilling to sell for less than 135p. Gulf have offered 105p and the current price stands at 120.5p. Just four shareholders control over 50 per cent of Clyde shares - Schroders, PDFM, Capital and Norwich Union.
-- BELL CABLEMEDIA PHONE ADS INCUR WRATH OF BT

British Telecom is heading for a legal battle with Bell Cablemedia over the latter's advertising campaign, which urges potential customers "Don't waste money - switch to cable" and includes posters with the slogan "British Telecon". BT lawyers are understood to have written to Bell warning them over the campaign.
